A road operator pays for each traffic sensor and covers only part of the network. We ask what sensors buy for the segments that have none. On three cities of the Traffic4cast benchmark, forecasting congestion in three classes 15–120 minutes ahead on segments the model never sees, we find no forecastable spatial information beyond the calendar at any coverage from 10\% to 60\%. A graph model gains nothing over the same model without its graph, and predictors without training do no better. Nearby labels do agree within about 250 m, but that agreement is shared calendar: a table of class frequencies by hour of the week forecasts as well as the trained model, and the neighbour's class adds nothing to it. Placement changes how close uncovered segments lie to a sensor, not how well they are forecast. What a sensor buys is the measurement at its own segment. For the loop detector, against independent speed references, that measurement detects congestion but does not measure its level. Every experiment was pre-registered and frozen, and the records, the predictions and one script that regenerates every number are released.
